What is the biggest problem caused by an inheritance or a will that you ever saw or heard about? Some years ago, when I was hunting for a house I found a property that seemingly had my name stamped on it. It was a neat little hillside property with two bedrooms that was built sturdily and with class. It was one of those good old-fashioned houses that was built in the 70s/80s with a cute porch and terrazzo flooring. The best part was it was within the mortgage the bank offered me. I called the owner and arranged for a proper tour. I brought my ex with me (who like most women, observed things men wouldn't notice) and we climbed the hill and waited in the yard for the owner to arrive. She then motioned to me that in the yard (just a few feet from one of the bedrooms) was this awful looking makeshift shack that looked to be someone's home. What we in Trinidad refer to as a 'Piper Shack.’ She told me that somebody was squatting on the property. I was really looking forward to getting the house and said the shack was probably just a storage shed. She then pointed to a DirectTV satellite on the roof and some crude plumbing that sent filthy water towards the main house. While contemplating all of this, a wild-looking man appeared out of nowhere and loudly greeted us. He told us the house we were interested is a great house and that so many people are interested in it. We then watched him as he entered the shack. I was completely disheartened but I said that this must be some guy hired to maintain the house temporarily. My ex called me a fool. That he was most obviously a squatter. Two men arrived and introduced themselves as the owners. They were pleasant and they spoke with warm conviction of how great the house was and how it was a shame that they were selling it for so low a price. They explained that they were cousins and the house was willed to them by their uncle who died recently. The uncle had no children of his own and left everything to his closest kin. The cousins, who had homes of their own decided to sell the house and split the money. The younger cousin then went on a tangent reminiscing about how nice their old uncle was and how much work he did on the house. 'And who's that man living in the back there,' my ex bluntly interjected. I could see disappointment swell up on the man's face. He obviously wanted to avoid the subject. He explained that his uncle had no one in his old age. He was unmarried and the nephews were grown and living their lives with their families. The uncle befriended a wandering drug addict (‘piper’ in Trinidad terms) and allowed for the man to build his shack in the yard, use his electricity and water and even included in the will that the man have rights to live there as long as he wants. 'But he's a real nice man when you get to know him!' the other cousin chimed in, 'He's very helpful with manual labor. He could watch after your house for you when you're away!’ It was such a sad sight to see them trying to pitch the idea that having a drug addicted, mentally unstable man living in your yard and with legal rights could actually be a good thing. They said that once we saw inside the house we'd see how great of a deal we were getting. In the end we decided that it wasn't worth our while and politely declined.

What one thing do you wish you had known about life when you were in your 20s? This question is for those who are older than 20 who would like to share their mistakes and insights with a younger person than themselves. I wish I didn’t get caught up in the typical young adult craze of getting a car. When I got my first full time job as a warehouse attendant at age 19, practically every male co-worker around this age would go philosophically deep in the discussion of buying their first car. A car meant everything to us simple minded fools. It signified freedom. It allowed for us to be able to go out wherever we wanted and come back home whenever we wanted. It meant getting premium birds (girls). It meant easier access to sex. It meant getting wasted on beers while bar-hopping and chilling out by the riverside or the beach with our closest pals. It meant blasting our favourite hit songs of the time while cruising through our neighbourhoods and getting attention. There was a certain mystique about getting a car at age 20 and to this day there still is. Now at 35, I can safely say that for the majority of 20 year olds, that mystique is in fact bull***t. There are only two criteria I believe that allows for getting a car at 20 to not be financial suicide. If you are fortunate to belong to either category, upon getting your first car Heaven’s Gate opens up and you have years of wild adventures at your helm that will allow for fond memories. If you don’t belong to either category, Heaven’s Gate opens up for an extremely short while but then suddenly the floor caves in on you and fall into the pits of finance hell that will allow for a bald spot on your head by age 23. Whether new or used, investing in a car at a young age is a recipe for disaster for the average Trinidadian 20 year old. When you’re fresh out of school and you decide to get a car to experience your man-child utopia, you might as well change the name of your bank account to your car’s license plate number. Practically all of your salary belongs to that car. If it’s new or foreign used (as we have in Trinidad) your ass is owned by whichever bank that gave you the loan for your car. You may cry ‘freedom at last’ to your parents but the bank has an even bigger leash around your neck and they don’t love you like mommy and daddy does. When you bite the bullet and save some money to buy a cheap, used car, you may pat yourself on the back for such grit and determination but you are most likely in a worse off position than your friend who has to pay a loan as your ass is owned by the mechanic. It’s almost pathetic to see the typical twenty something year old Trini looking frantic at the side of the road after his car broke down; no money to pay for a wrecking service, desperate for any kind of assistance, his lady-friend abandoning him in shame. Yet I see such a scenario every Friday evening, especially when I pass by the mall. Friends and peers would make the excuse, ‘Once you choose a good car and have a really good mechanic you could buy a used car.’ I fell for this terrible piece of advice and at age 24 bought with cash my first car. It was used and recommended by a trusted mechanic friend. It was one of these: It was a disaster. I had a breakdown the very second day of driving it. I spent more time waiting for the mechanic to fix it than actually driving it. The steering wheel actually came off while driving one fine evening. Going on a date while driving this beauty was more suspenseful than a Hitchcock movie; will it break down on me and roll down the hill? Oh no, what’s that weird noise? When I had to get repairs/service done, sourcing parts for my discontinued model would send me on an Indiana Jones like expedition where I would find myself in some remote scrap-yard miles away from home, climbing up a ghastly stack of aged and abandoned vehicles looking for a model like mine. If I was lucky enough to find my model, the scrap yard owner would gauge how desperate I looked and charged to suit. Forget starting a small business, forget marrying your sweetheart, ignore stock market opportunities, partnerships or simply taking a summer trip to Cancun. My beaten up Ford Laser was my business partner, my lover, my future, my everything. Forget taking out girls to movies and the beach, I might as well carry out my mechanic and try to sweetheart him into cheaper rates. The final straw came when I took out my last bit of money from my account and was siphoning some from my credit card, an epiphany ocurred: At the time, my mechanic informed me that he was unavailable but his son would take over duties for the time being. As I waited at the garage for the son to arrive, I saw a boy, a few years younger than me, ride towards me with his bicycle and park it at the garage. Wondering if the kid was lost or confused, I told him that this was a garage for cars, not bikes. He laughed and said that he was the mechanic. I queried why he didn't have a car, being a mechanic and all. He gave me a knowing glance and said, ‘Can’t afford one.’ ‘But there are so many cheap used cars for sale!?’ I said quite fascinated, ‘And you know how to fix ‘em!?’ He simply smiled and said nothing. He asked me to raise my bonnet. I then realized he probably saw me as a fool. He had already given his answer. Just because he could fix them himself doesn’t mean that they would stop being a bloody expense, a pain in the ass and a sacrifice of all other youthful goals and endeavours. It was time to face the facts, buying a used car, for someone like me, was like buying a dying horse. After the repair I put the car for sale at a great loss and washed my hands of it. Something magical happened after. Like glimmering grass on a summer morning, I could see my money starting to grow. Life suddenly became enjoyable again. Whenever I see a twenty year old posing proudly next to his aged, first car, I shake my head and laugh to myself. The amount of money he is going to spend behind that vehicle could clothe and feed a child. Go ahead and call it your baby.

What jobs will most likely still be around in 1000 years? Plumbers most definitely. My plumber is 82 years old and he still gets work. I should call him to check and see if he's still alive. But jokes aside plumbers will always be in demand. Why? So when the end of the world is near and we have to select a few people to inhabit another planet let's all make sure we keep a few good plumbers on board.

What Scorsese film would have been better if directed by Spielberg and vice versa? Interesting question. In regards to Spielberg doing a Scorsese film, I know I may be in a minority but I never had much love for Scorsese's Gangs of New York (2002). I've never been able to sit through the entire film. In my honest opinion, just because the epoch the film is based on is an ugly period in history, it doesn’t mean that the film has to be inherently ugly. In the comparable and far superior Once Upon A Time in America (1984), Sergio Leone captures the pockets of childhood innocence and warm camaraderie in a truly poetic manner despite the inherent ugliness of the period documented. In Gangs of New York everywhere looked like a filthy trash heap. All the main characters were assholes. Everyone was somehow dressed in the most rattiest rags they could find. I think Scorsese was a little heavy handed in demonstrating the chaotic grittiness of the period. With the exception of Daniel Day Lewis the entire cast gave mediocre performances. The colours and camera work of the cinematography was glaring and unsettling and the whole revenge arc story didnt seem to have much of a point in the context it was used. In a nutshell the film was just a pointless, ugly film that just happened to have a measure of historical accuracy. Spielberg is the King of demonstrating the humanity that can be found in the absolute darkest periods of history. He does this without undermining historical accuracy or succumbing to fluffy melodrama. Of course the chief examples being Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan. I think if Spielberg was given the job to direct Gangs of New York, the final product would've been a superior film with fleshed out, relatable characters, a better plot and overall a much more engaging experience for the senses. In regards to Scorsese doing a Spielberg film, I think the there is one film that was right up Scorsese’s alley that I think Spielberg’s did a disservice. Scorsese's eye for realism and portraying characters in their raw, unlikable form would've created a better product. No. It's not Munich (2005) It's Catch Me if You Can. The film was a the feelgood blockbuster movie of 2002. Frank Abagnale Jr was the antihero everyone couldn’t help but love, especially when portrayed by hearthtrob Leonardo DiCaprio. I enjoyed the movie when it premiered but it has aged poorly as of recently. Abagnale Jr was not just a scammer, it has been revealed that he is also a pathological liar. Much of the events described in his book are either grossly exaggerated or completely untrue. When you watch the film now you are treated to a self-indulgent, ego-stroking feast of fakery. I think Scorsese would've been a bit more skeptical towards the author's story and do the proper research into Abagnale Jr's life. The story would've been less attractive and a lot more cynical with moments of downright nastiness (very much in the vein of Raging Bull and The Wolf of Wall Street) but it might have been a compelling portrait of a fractured individual who thought more of himself than he actually was. It definitely wouldn't have the embarrassment that Catch Me if You Can suffers from today. So in conclusion, Spielberg and Scorsese should’ve simply traded director seats in the year 2002.

Can you name an actor who was never a good actor but became one? Sterling Hayden never wanted to be an actor. He was coaxed into the profession as a young, handsome sailor whose photogenic good looks appealed to a post WWII audience who were just begging for actors who were the image of tall and rugged manliness. The 6′5 blonde, athletic young shipmate got into the industry after a 1938 photo gained popularity in a fisherman's magazine. Dubbed by Paramount as 'The Beautiful Blond Viking God’ he got into the industry as a means to purchase his own ship but grew to resent Hollywood. His early roles were a slew of rather forgettable Westerns and film noirs. After his role in the classic Western Johnny Guitar starring Joan Crawford he became a bonafide star. However around this time his personal life got more attention as he was reported to have communist sympathies during the McCarthy/Red Scare era and during a vicious custody battle for his children he took his four children on a self manned trip aboard his ship Wanderer from San Francisco Bay to Tahiti despite the legal implications that awaited him at home. His impulsive nature, hatred of Hollywood,anti- capitalism sentiments and sometimes reckless behaviour gave him the image of an eccentric, of which is well documented in his autobiography Wanderer (1963). However upon working with Stanley Kubrick in The Killing he found his niche playing manic and impulsive characters, not far removed from his actual personality. His best role arguably being that of the insane American General Jack D. Ripper in Kubrick's classic black political comedy Dr. Strangelove. His final great role was that of corrupt Irish police Captain Mark McCluskey in The Godfather (1972). Despite the critical and commercial resurgence his roles and his writings were used solely to fund his travels of which (along with legal expenses and taxes) he continuously saw his money decrease. He died of prostate cancer at the of 70 in 1986, leaving behind six children.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? Balram. There was a boy who came from the depths of poverty named Balram. He was sinewy and had coarse skin and features that made him look like he jumped out of the pages of our history books as an indentured laborer from colonial times. Everything about him was out of sync with the rest of the class. This was the late 90s and baggy pants were the thing, Balram wore his khaki trousers wrapped tight around his skinny legs. Perms from excessive hair gel (my specialty at the time), corn-rows, Caesar styled and spiky hair was the rage amongst teenage boys back then. Balram wore something that looked straight out of a an old Amitabh Bachchan movie from the 70s. Balram's school uniforms always looked faded and threadbare. Never once did anyone see him wearing new items of clothing. This led to many of the kids in class poking fun at the possibility that Balram's family got used clothes for him. Balram didn't have cable. It was possible he didn't have a TV. Balram didn't care for the music everyone else listened to. He didn't go to the arcade and play video games. He didn't get excited hearing about Stone Cold Steve Austin. He was odd in that he only enjoyed games that demonstrated his eerie strength and his skills in survival. This included holding breath competitions, arm wrestling, 'mercy’ and 'bokee' (hitting an opponents fist by flicking a finger against it until someone gives up in pain). He didn't have much of a sense of humour. He would sit in class like an old Native American chief, peering knowingly at the world through his squinted, Charles Bronson-esque eyes while everyone else made jokes and acted like morons who needed attention. My friends and I would hang out with him but for some reason he never was an official member of our group. He preferred to roam alone. Once, I was tricked by some boys into pretending to want to beat him up, all for kicks. Before I could say 'Hey' Balram lifted me into the air by the shoulders and against the wall until I yielded. It was an impressive display of brute strength that I could never forget. In moments of boredom Balram was usually an easy target for jokes and insults. Some of the girls were particularly mean to him. One would say to that she would never be with a boy like him who looks dirty and always smells like old curry. The boys would always joke around that he came from 'the bush’ and came to school swinging on vines like Tarzan. One of the boys even managed to create a comic depicting Balram's life in the bush, fighting snakes and tigers on a daily basis etc. Balram learned to laugh with everyone and not let it get to him. In Form 3 Balram vanished. Always a recluse he never communicated to anyone what were his plans/intentions. Some months later he visited the school wearing a new uniform and with a friend at his side. He got transferred to a school closer to home where more rural kids like him were around. He looked much happier and was far more social than he was before. That day, most of the class ignored him but my friends and I held a reception to commemorate the good times we had with him. He said his new school was the best; teachers were hardly there and the kids did what they wanted. He showed me a tattoo that he got on his arm of a dragon. Even though the tattoo looked ridiculously amateurish and his clothes were still faded and threadbare and his hair still outdated my friends and I sang his praises and gave him his day. He really was a great guy. He had no fear of trying to fit in and had an infinite amount of patience for those around him. I wouldn't be surprised to find out that he made a huge success out if his life as an adult. But alas that day was the last time I saw him/heard anything about him.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? Self-Help Books Can Actually Ruin Your Life Especially if you come from a developing country. Have you ever sat and pondered as to the staggering amount of self-help authors there are out there? It seems every week someone is recommending to you some brand new, groundbreaking, best selling title that eschews a whole new perspective on how to view the world and live your life. The problem with 99% of the authors: Are they really living their dreams? Or are they making a living selling dreams? Moulding a life of success, solely based on easily digestible tips, hints and formulae is like solving advanced level algebra, whilst riding a roller coaster, using only your knowledge of multiplication tables. The knowledge can help….you probably might get the most simple problems correct……but it would be ridiculous to think that you would be able to solve all your problems in that manner, under those unique circumstances. These are people living in dire poverty in India. What can I do to help them out of this financial rut?….. I know! Think and Grow Rich by Napoleon Hill A lonely, mentally unhinged taxi driver… That's easy. The Road Less Travelled and How to Win Friends and Influence People. A wealthy but socially and emotionally void and suicidal philanthropist. Hmm. That's a tough one….The Alchemist by Paolo Coelho and you can throw in The Prophet by Gibran as well. Nothing cures rich-man depression more than obscure but romanticised Eastern parables and fables. Ok, so it's foolish to try and live according to a self help book, but how can I ruin my life simply by seeking advice? In every job that I've worked, every year there's always that one newly employed guy who is all jacked up from reading a lifetime's supply of self help books. He is always brimming with confidence and eager to pin his obstacles against the ropes and send failure scattering with his 2000 watt grin. He hates to hear no and scorns to see people second guessing themselves. He wants to take on all life's challenges and has a Napoleon Hill or Robert Kiyosaki quote ready for every situation. Then something inexplicable happens. Something gradually builds up, registers in his subconscious and overflows upon his ego. It usually takes the form of this mental conversation. 'Wait a minute. I've done everything the book advised me to. I've followed the instructions to the hilt…….yet I'm not seeing the results.’ He hasn't been promoted by his supervisor, rather his supervisor has been taking credit for his own efforts and is getting the promotion instead. Despite constantly showing support and empathy, his wife is even more nagging and helpless than when he first met her. His dedication to go above and beyond with the customer now has him doing the workload of all the lazy and incompetent coworkers around him, who still draw the same salary. He gets the lion's share of verbal abuse from disgruntled customers who rather voice their issues with him rather than the incompetent coworkers. His small business as a landscaper is suffering because his fair price is being exploited whilst mediocre landscapers are charging abominably overpriced rates and are getting more work than him. What the hell is happening here? He followed some great and timeless advice. He just forget to put in one small factor in his equation. His personal environment. His ever changing, ever complex, personal environment. The variable that if included onto his scientific calculator would produce the answer E or 'Error.’ In developing countries likes Trinidad, using US or English or German translated or Dutch translated or any developed country self help books can cause ruin your life because the environment is so different. In developing countries: These are all factors that contradict with what he read in his books and come only through experience. Had he been all the wiser he would've known that not every bit of advice in his self help books could be applied to his unique situation and environment. To make matters worse nowadays, everybody is a self help author and rather than have synchronized, compatible, time tested advice, we have polarising, wishy-washy, one-size-fits-all concoctions and psudo-psychological, parabolic gibberish. Basically, self help authors write anecdotes that's easy to understand, easy to apply and appealing to the majority. Below is a list of a few popular modern self help authors and their most famous philosophy: Robert Kiyosaki: If you have to lose, lose spectacularly. Malcolm Gladwell: You have within you an instinct to know when something 'feels’ like a rip-off. Jay Shetty: Think like a monk. Deepak Chopak: Thinking is like brain chemistry. Steve Harvey: Act like a lady, think like a man Paolo Coelho: The universe…

What screams "I'm educated, but not very bright"? I bought an old car that needed some work some time back. I brought it over to a friend of the family who recently started a mechanic shop and I thought it would be a nice gesture to give him the job to look over the basic servicing the car needed. He was no ordinary junkyard mechanic. This guy was educated. He sought after practically every certificate that was available in automotive repair and technology. He would watch countless videos on the latest trends in the automotive industry and could engage you in long conversation as to what is the best model car and brand to invest in at the moment. His father was a highly venerated machinist and from that he learned how to give engine heads the perfect optimization for power\speed etc. All that was fine and grand but I just wanted the basic servicing for my old vehicle; check the oil, brakes, suspension, steering etc etc. On the day that he told me to collect the vehicle I came to his garage and saw him sprawled on the floor next to the disassembled wheels looking as though he just heard news the love of his life had died. I asked him what was wrong. He said that he couldn’t figure out exactly why the brake pads weren’t fitting in the caliper no matter how hard he tried. He said that he even broke the clips of two pads trying to force them in and had to buy new ones (to my expense of course). ‘I’ve never had a problem like this before. I don’t know what’s going on. This is insane.’ He said this as though he suffered a crushing defeat at Waterloo. Now I don’t know anything about cars myself and I’m just the ordinary layman who could jumpstart, change his own tire, fuses etc. If this guy who held so many certificates in auto mechanics couldn’t figure out what was wrong with this caliper then something was seriously wrong with this car. I felt very upset that I made such a bad purchase. I then took a look at the caliper in question and immediately I saw the problem. ‘Why don’t you take out the old brake pads in the caliper to make space for the new ones?’ The ‘huh’ look that appeared on his face I could never forget. He took out the old ones and slapped in the new without any issue or further delay. I was flabbergasted. I was wondering if it was a good idea to carry this vehicle to him in the first place. He was intelligent but apparently he wasn’t very bright. The answer to my question came when I tried starting the car but got nothing when I turned the key. I watched him as he panicked and wondered what was the problem this time. He did everything right to his knowledge. ‘Isn’t that my battery over there?’ I said pointing to what looked like my car battery in the corner. ‘Right, right’ he said, ‘The battery.’ The bugger charged $1500 for his labour even though afterwards I found out that he didn’t clamp the exhaust back up properly and it fell down while driving. I had to tie it back to the chassis with some binding wire that I was lucky to have in the trunk. I owe him $500. He’ll be waiting a very long time until he gets that money.

What "poverty food" is actually really delicious? Trinidad has many types of delicious poverty meals that stem from colonialism, slavery and East Indian indentureship. Some are despondently looked upon with embarassment while others are now expensive delicacies that tourists pay, 'ah pound and ah crown’ for. Poor poverty meals These are the meals that really represent someone going through hard times. These are the delicacies prepared from the remnants of the pantry and hunger induced experimentation. Rice and butter As the name suggests, boiled rice grains soaked in butter. Actually it's not butter but margarine, as real butter here is more expensive than most meats. Exceedingly unhealthy but much more delicious than you would imagine. Just imagine the taste of mashed potatoes except it's rice. Flour porridge Heat some white flour on a skillet and just before it's about to burn throw in some condensed milk and water. This is a Haitian recipe but used by many older Trinis who want to feel full but can't afford to buy groceries. According to how well you garnish this concoction, it can be a hidden delight. Plain egg rice When you have one egg and a bag of rice and you need to feed an entire family, this is the meal of choice. Basically you heat up some boiled rice and throw in a well beaten egg. You will be astonished at how far one egg can stretch. Green fig (banana) with ‘butter’ and salt A family with a couple of banana trees in the yard could be saved from starvation with this simple, delicious meal. Boil a couple full but unripe bananas (with or without skin) and serve with margarine and salt. A fully developed green fig well soaked in margarine with a dash of salt can beat meals in most 5 star restaurants. Banana fritters Instead of throwing away your near rotted bananas, mash them to a pulp, knead in some flour and deep fry in oil. Even when eaten cold these fritters are a treat. Rich Poverty Meals These were meals made from ingredients the upper class and colonial masters would discard such as chickens’ neck and pig's tail. Now they are culinary delights that tourists flock towards and are quite expensive to make/purchase. Chicken Foot souse Don't run away just yet. This flavor will knock your socks off. This is basically boiled chicken's feet soaked in a zesty broth. You'd be surprised the amount of meat a chicken's foot can give. Geera neck Dont throw away those chicken necks! Season them with cumin roast them on a skillet for a spicy snack. These are popular 'cutters’ or bar foods, made to sober up drunkards. This can be made with chicken gizzards also. Fried chicken livers My mother would carry us to this seedy looking bakery on a Sunday where they served fried chicken livers, mostly to satisfy the patrons of the bar that was situated next to them. You'll spit out its overly pungent flavor at first try but it gets tastier after each bite. Pig tail Pig tail meals are now synonymous with special events such as birthday parties and wedding receptions. Pig tail pelau, as shown above, is made from rice and pig tails cooked in caramelized sugar (stewed) with peas and whatever garnishes desired. There is also pig tail soup. A pig's tail is incredibly meaty, tender and juicy that so much that many people find themselves sucking at the bone upon finishing. Black pudding Thanks to our English rulers of yesteryear who brought this excrement looking sausage, made entirely of pig's blood, to the Caribbean. Our version includes a lot more spices and this dish is quite popular served in bread as a street food. It looks and sounds horrid but it is quite creamy textured and rich in taste. and lastly Cow heel soup Who would've known that a cow's heel would be so gelatinous, meaty and soak up flavour so well. Along with fish broth and corn soup, this is the definitive soup of Trinidad.

Is it superficial that I lost interest in a guy because he proudly said that he hasn't read any book in his life? Here's the point of view of a somewhat bookish male. First of all I would say that you've started wrong by considering something he claims about himself. A man (a many women in general) will say all kinds of things to give some kind of impression. In his case he is bragging that he doesn't like books/reading. He probably comes from a rugged environment where reading books is looked down upon as dandyish, antisocial and/or overly sensitive. I come from such an environment. Trinidad is a literate country but for males the stereotypical clumsy, scatterbrained geek who hides behind books because he is afraid to tackle worldly experiences is a prominent stigma. Even if you speak meticulously with proper English words that contain more than two syllables you are regarded with suspicion. Many females are raised to avoid these type of men. Him being proud not reading books is, to me, an ego driven declaration of machismo. You shouldn't let that be a deciding factor though. When younger I always sought after intellectual type girls with whom I could discuss the arts, philosophy, politics, classic literature etc. Sadly relationships never seemed too work out with for a myriad of reasons the chief problem being a severe lack of emotional intelligence. Now that I'm older, the last quality I look for in a woman in how much books she has read in life. Literacy and intelligence are two completely different types of wisdom and I would argue that the latter is far more important than the former. Just because he doesn't read doesn't mean he is any less wise, thoughtful, caring and responsible than the average guy. I've met too many literate women who are a financial and emotional trainwreck to allow for the notion that book reading is a make or break factor in a relationship. Just my two cents.

What was your first clue you were no longer as young as you thought you were? While working in a school library I was at the computers assisting some students in finishing their assignments to submit to their teachers. Most students would email their assignments to their teacher, others (who didn't have/couldn't remember their email address) would save it on a USB flash drive . This one student who had neither an email address or a flash drive raised his hand for assistance and told me of his situation. I went into our storage cupboard and brought out an old rewritable CD-RW; the kind I used back in school to copy (‘burn’ as we used to call it) data onto. I gave him the shiny disc and walked off assuming that he knew what to do with it. ‘Sir!’ I heard his voice call after me. ‘Yeah?’ ‘What am I supposed to do with this?’ ‘Burn it,’ I said and looked at him stoically. His friends started laughing believing that I was teasing. ‘Sir stop joking. I need to save my work.’ ‘Burn the work onto the CD’ I said and he started to look at me irritated. ‘Sir help him out. Stop joking’ one of the friends said. It then dawned on me that they had no idea what ‘burning a CD’ was. This was before their time. I proceeded to demonstrate to them how to copy data onto a CD-RW, feeling like a crusty old man giving them a tour on a private railroad. The sad thing was they were all 16–17 and I wasn't much older at 24.

What are some unintentionally rude things people say and do? Oh man! Try this experiment at your workplace or if you don’t work, in the neighborhood/apartment complex where you live. Go to the grocery and get a large box. Make sure the top lid is closed and walk around with it. If 7 out of 10 people that you are familiar with don’t ask you, ‘Hey what’s in the box?’ I’m a monkey’s uncle. How about this. Dress up really nice one day. Not like you’re going to pick up an award but just put some extra effort in looking good with your best clothes, new haircut/hairdo etc. If 7 out of 10 people that you are familiar with don’t ask you, ‘Hey. How come you’re all dressed up. You got a hot date later or something?’ Then I’m the King of Spain. Or even this most simple one. Don’t use your car to go to work/the grocery but rather use a taxi/Uber or whatever. If practically everyone who you’re familiar with doesn’t ask you, ‘Hey. What happened to your car?’ then you have my permission to shave my head bald and call me Biscuit. My point is that people think it’s ok to be nosey for every insignificant change they see about others. If someone you know is walking around with a box. Leave them alone. Boxes exist. People utilize them all the time. It’s none of your business to know what he/she has inside. If someone dresses up extra special one day, they have their own personal reason why. They don’t have to explain anything to you. It could be their anniversary, or a day or some personal significance or they just feel like dressing up nice for a change. If someone decides not to use their car, what’s it to you? Unless you are their mechanic then it’s none of your business. They could probably just not want to drive that day or they could’ve loaned the car to someone or they’re getting it sold. Why is it any of your business? People have this odd desire to see others perform the same routine every day. It’s like if you do something slightly different it disorients them and they need an explanation why. So by and large I would say that without a doubt the most widespread and pervasive act of rudeness that is allowed in society is being overly mindful of our fellow men’s personal affairs.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? The Founder (2016) This is a movie I habitually return to watching. It's an inspiring movie but it's not a ‘feelgood’ movie per se. The movie tells the story of how a run of the mill salesman named Ray Kroc outmanoeuvred and outperformed the McDonald brothers and became owner of the McDonald's franchise/empire. I say it's not feelgood because, based on the film, Kroc was not by any account a ‘nice’ man when it came to business. He was a conniving opportunist but at the same time he was also unrelentingly persistent. His partners, the altruistic McDonald brothers derived a brilliant concept and product but had little interest in franchising and/or wealth. It is because of Kroc's persistence and willingness to take great risks that McDonald's is the success that it is today. If there is one concept the movie begs you to take away from it, regardless of your view of Ray Kroc, it is the value of persistence. Without giving away too much of the plot, this is what is inspiring about Kroc's efforts. There are so many profound scenes and quotes in this movie that it find it hard for anyone to not appreciate it for the sole merit that it generates a lot of thought, regardless of whether you don't like it or find Ray Kroc reprehensible. I think Michael Keaton gave his greatest performance and I was thoroughly disappointed that he was not nominated for an Academy Award. His persistence speech at the end of the film, I consider to be a classic in business motivation, trumping that of Jordan Belfort’s ‘sell me this pen’ in The Wolf of Wall Street and Alec Baldwin's ‘Always be closing’ scene in Glengarry Glen Ross. I beg to debate this opinion.

What is the most shocking thing you have seen your mother do? Around age 7 or 8 my mother sent me off to school with a brand new pencil case full of sparkling new stationery. Coming from a school full of children of limited means, having brand new stuff was a big deal, especially at the middle of the school term. Classmates would gather round and gaze in awe at your virgin erasers that smelt almost delicious, sharperners with shiny, sharp blades, clear plastic rulers so new you could look through them and make your classmates look taller or shorter according to the angle etc, etc. However the most prided item in my pencil case was my pencil. It was painted a glossy, emerald green and crafted of premium quality wood that gave a musky fragrance. For a class of post-toddlers this never before seen pencil was exceedingly impressive. Everyone ooh-ed and ahh-ed at my 2B Excalibur. I was King for a day…or at least for a few hours. Apparently the meanest, most scoundrel-iest boy in class, Stefan, didn’t like the fact that I was getting so much attention. Stefan came from a troubled background. He had an extensive vocabulary of all forms of obscene language and was extremely disrespectful to the point that he would perversely hold conversations discussing what the genitalia of our female teachers was like. Because of his shocking nature none of the other boys would ever challenge him as we had the juvenile belief that the more filthy the mouth, the more dangerous the boy. Coming back to class after lunch I found Stefan perusing through my bag without my permission. I asked him what he was doing and saw that he had my precious pencil in his hands. ‘I need your pencil borrow,’ he said with great pathos, ‘I didn't do the homework last night and I have no pencil. Miss (the teacher) will beat me if she find out.’ Although I found it strange that Stefan was suddenly interested in his homework and I knew for a fact that our teacher didn't care what Stefan did with his homework book as long as he kept his filthy mouth shut during class, I allowed him use of my pencil. With a heavy heart I watched as a smug smile developed on his face and he proceeded to eye the glossy green paint and sniff at the shaven wood. Some minutes afterwards, while class was in process, Stefan, who was seated directly behind me, could be heard making a weird crunching noise. I looked behind me and recoiled in horror at the most devastating sight my innocent eyes ever beheld. My precious pencil was in Stefan's mouth. Not only that, it was broken in half and he had split one of the halves down the centre with his teeth and was in the process of doing the same with the other half. Although fully aware of the futility of the matter, like a kneejerk I grabbed at my pencil pieces but Stefan evaded my attempt. I could see a cruel Chesire grin spread on on his mouth. He spat out the pieces and said while laughing, ‘The pencil point broke……I needed to get the lead inside.` The teacher demanded for us to explain why we were joking around in class and in tears I ran to her and explained the entire story, how Stefan was caught prying inside my bag, took my pencil without permission, lied and now broke it into pieces. ‘Return to your seat Elijah,’ the teacher said angrily, ‘It's just a pencil. Stop crying like a little girl.’ Stefan and the rest of the class burst out into laughter. I returned to my seat full of anger and remorse. I struggled to fight the tears from flowing. I couldnt speak to anyone for the rest of the day. When I went home I immediately went to my mother and released all those pent up tears and explained the story in great detail. My mother didn’t say anything except ask for the name of the culprit and the name of my teacher. The following day I returned to school in a morose mood. Stefan saw me enter class and began to tease me about crying over a pencil like a little girl. Two hours later, the Principal entered our class and whispered to our teacher and left. The teacher had a stunned look on her face and angrily told Stefan to follow her out the classrom. Ten minutes later Stefan resumed his place looking as though he had just been handed a life sentence. The teacher returned and proceeded to give a speech in which she stated that anyone caught going into another student's belongings would be sent to the Principal and possibly suspended. She mentioned the incident with Stefan and me and explained that Stefan's mother was contacted and had promised to replace the pencil that Stefan stole and destroyed. The following day I recieved a generic replacement pencil from Stefan. He looked me in the eyes and said in a serious but pleading tone, ‘Don't ever call your mother for me again Elijah.’ I told him I didnt know what he was talking about. He told me that yesterday he came into the staff room with the teacher to see this little lady, my mother, acting crazy and talking about going to the police about something. He said that my mother had told the staff room that my grandmother had put $100 in my book bag for me to carry home to her to buy groceries and it was missing. My mother demanded to know why teachers were allowing stealing to happen in front of their eyes. ‘Elijah. Tell your mother I never touched your money.’ Stefan passionately interjected as he told the story, ‘I only take the pencil and that's all.’ He continued the story. ‘No student here stole any money from your son Miss,’ the Principal had said stoically, ‘We do not tolerate theft here.’ ‘If a student didn’t steal the money,’ my mother had replied, ‘Somebody had to have stolen it.’ This of course subtly alleging that my teacher had stolen the money. There was a rabble amongst the teachers and the matter ended with the Principal taking $50 from his wallet and urging other teachers to contribute to make up for the ‘lost’ $100. In the end, $80 was donated from the teachers to my mother, who said thanks but still was upset over the theft. I thought about all that I heard and couldnt make sense of it. Grandma had died years ago. ‘I didn't know I had $100 in my bag!’ I said defensively to Stefan. ‘I don't care,’ Stefan cried, ‘Just keep your mother away from me.’ He was genuinely terrified of my little mother. When I went home that evening I was pleasantly surprised to see my precious 2B Excalibur was waiting for me. My mother had bought another to replace the one Stefan broke and a little toy car and she managed to cook my favorite meal of spaghetti and meatballs that day. Aware of our financial position I asked how she managed to buy all this. She told me it was courtesy of the school. I then told her about the story Stefan gave me about the missing $100 in my bag. She explained that no one in the school would've taken her seriously if she quarrelled about a pencil, regardless if it was a pencil as nice as mine. ‘Then you lied to the teachers and the Principal.’ I said rather shocked. ‘I didn’t lie,’ she said, ‘I exaggerated. Stefan did go into your bag without permission. Stefan did take your pencil without permission. Stefan did lie about using your pencil for homework. The teacher didn't repimand Stefan for his actions. The teacher did mock you and cause emotional damage. If there was $100 in your bag, a boy like Stefan would've definitely stolen it. I embellished the truth so that they could see the seriousness of the matter. Now justice is served.’ I had no idea what she was talking about. She was a big fan of Matlock back then and was talking lawyer talk. In my mind I was shocked that my mother lied to coerce my school into giving us money but as I grew into a teenager I understood better what she did. People sue for far more petty matters, tell much more sensational exagerrations and get rewarded fortunes. That is how the law works. As for Stefan, never heard a peep from him again. The event made him so notorious that he was placed to sit in the back of the class away from me or any other susceptible victims. It's unfair to him, I know, but his mother should've watched Matlock also.

The Good, the Bad & the Ugly is an amazing movie but I never understood the scene involving Tuco and his monk brother. As much as it was an emotional scene, it did not advance the movie plot at all. Did Leone ever explain why he added the scene? Yeah. Quite true. But then again, remember, throughout the movie, how often Tuco does this: Everytime he kills or someone is killed through his double crossing, he makes a sign of the Cross. Clearly he has a conflicted relationship with God. It paves the way for the reveal that he comes from a very religious background i.e. the scene with his disapproving monk brother. Admittedly, that scene sticks out like a sore thumb. I guess it was to give an emotional depth to Tuco`s character. It was meant to show that Tuco had a sympathetic, human side to him. Blondie had an emotional side as evident by the short scene where he shared his cigarette with the young, dying soldier. That scene was perfection. However Tuco`s emotional scene didn't play out so well. It tried a tad too hard. Tuco was well characterized and even without this scene one could sense that though he was bad, he wasn't evil. Tuco kept odd standards of decency, unlike Angel Eyes who was a psychopath. Before the monk scene, the movie had established a macho aesthetic of manly indifference. These guys were looking for gold, not for emotional closure. Then this overwrought scene comes in and goes on too long and is a bit unlike Tuco`s persona. He was too hardened from years of crime and debauchery to care about the opinion of his monk brother who he considered a fool or even his recently deceased father who he obviously didn't have a good relationship with. If I were Leone I would write the scene as Tuco`s brother (who is not a monk) informing him that he is headed towards their father`s funeral and grudgingly invites Tuco to pay his final respect. Tuco, feeling a bit remorseful and embarrassed considers the offer but reflects upon the possibility of Blondie escaping and the lost chance of getting gold, makes an excuse and declines. It would be less than 2 minutes long. But it isn’t too off putting and that is why to this day it's still my favorite movie of all time.

What is your review of The Banshees of Inisherin? Watched this last Saturday with my girlfriend who thought it looked fascinating. Reading the two other reviews I agree with both as they mention that as a film it remains with you. To this hour it is still slowly digesting into my subconscious. I must stress on the word slow though. That is one of the biggest issues I had with the film. There's slow burner, where something is supposed to happen to connect the dots and then there's just slow, where there is little to no point. It's just slow for being slow's sake. That's the case with Banshees imho. The film posits the reason for the slowness being that Inisherin is a remote isle off Ireland and it's the 1920s. There is no electricity and the isle is so dull best friends no longer speaking could make front page news. This is actually the basis of the plot. Colin Farrel's Pádraic and Brendon Gleeson's Colm are no longer on speaking terms. Pádraic wants to continue idle chatting over beers in the pub while Colm wants more in life. This sets the stage for a series of surreal events that's supposed to be a mataphor for Irish Republicanism or something or the other. It is at that point where the film started losing me slowly. The cast is great, particularly Colin Farrell's slow-witted but good natured character who reminds me of George W Bush at times. He hits the nail on the head as a middle-aged, needy, ineffectual drunk. The cinematography is pretty and it does give a genuine sense of a place lost in time exactly one century ago. However both my girlfriend and I felt as though there was really no point. In beating on the head its symbolism and satire the movie missed out on what could've been a truly good period piece. My rating ** out of 4.

What is something Supernatural that you Witnessed, that you know no one would believe you about? My aunt and uncle left me alone in their house a night as they went to have their anniversary dinner. I was around 13 years old and felt like a King for that brief moment. After helping myself to many of their premium snacks my stomach churned and I needed to go use the toilet. While I was sitting there a strange phenomenon occured. Directly ahead of me a single ceiling tile lifted upwards, then the one in front of it, then another and another. In a straight line they lifted, with half second intervals. Outside of the bathroom and along the hallway I could hear the procession of lifted ceiling tiles. There was no wind outside. Even if there was, several tiles would've been lifted and rattled all at once in a brief flurry. I could think of no plausible explanation that could make ceiling tiles lift upwards in a singular straight line procession with half second intervals. No animal could cause tiles to be lifted in that manner unless they crawled/walked about with suction shoes of sorts. When it finally stopped I was numb with fear. The event had allowed for my bowels to unintentionally finish its duty much faster than usual. After, I ran out the bathroom and waited in the kitchen where the entrance door was located. When my Aunt and Uncle returned I frantically explained to them the entire story sparing no detail. In shock I watched as they began to laugh at my story and nonchalantly pour themselves a nightcap as they readied themselves to retire to bed. They didn't seem to take it serious at all. My aunt eyed me looking solemn and appeared to have considered my story for a few seconds. 'Did you flush the toilet Elijah?’ Did I? Everything happened in a blur. I ran to the bathroom and saw that in fact I didn't. I felt humiliated as I flushed. It felt like my experience was flushed also. Such is the sad reality of 13 yr old boys like myself trying to convey supernatural experiences to their dismissive relatives.

What should I absolutely not do when visiting your country? TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO Avoid hiring 'local tour guides.’ Stick to official touring groups from your hotel or large hiking groups. You’ve come to Trinidad on a vacation but you don't want to be so 'touristy.’ You don't want to sign up for the generic cross country tour the hotel is offering. You don't want to be crammed in a bus with a bunch of khaki short wearing, middle aged couples who want to stop the bus every 10 minutes saying. 'Hey driver, look there's a natural spring there. I want to fill my water bottle.’ Or 'Ooh driver stop the bus. I want to get a picture of those local Trinidadian cows.’ And you definitely don't want to go on the same well beaten hiking track where ten buses like yours are parked so more tourists like yourself could commence on a 5 minute hike, past dozens of souvenir stalls, to see a dormant mud volcano which, if you're lucky, might belch out a nauseating scent of rotten eggs. It sounds awful but believe me the other option is far worse. You'd meet someone who'd tell you, 'I know a guy who does private tours. He'll take you to the real hidden sites that the tour groups don't go and he's very knowledgeable of history and professional. You don't have to stick with the dull tourist tours.’ You want to make the extra effort and discover the hidden Trinidad (or Tobago) and this guy sounds like the real deal. Here are the problems with that offer: Discovering a makeshift stone axe . My Scottish cousins realized this too late when they hired some guy who was a friend of a friend of friend who did private tours. He was taking them to Turure Water Steps which was indeed a beautiful place with four amazing waterfalls, each bigger than the last. When I heard he was charging $1000 TT (roughly 150 US) to take them there I protested and told them that they were being ripped off. Anyone could take them there for free. They argued that he was a professional and had deep knowledge of the history of places. I went along with them for the trip. Some hours later, returning home, they agreed that they were ripped off. In summary the lesson learned here is that there are several people like that so-called tour guide who wants to rip off hapless tourists. Either you stick with your hotel tour or if you want to go off the beaten track, join a professional hiking/tour group or go with a large group of friendly, trustworthy locals. Doing otherwise could have you ripped off or even worse. Edit 31.08.21 Had no idea this little tidbit of info would've garnered so many upvotes. Thank you all for the support. Here are some more images of Turure. If you enjoyed this I can assume that you enjoy travel. Check out my piece on the island of Dominica, a pristine, little island lost in time. Click here.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? This is actually my childhood favourite and I'm certain he's the hero of many a boy born in the 20th century. He's a cunning, worldly lad who lives with his aunt and half brother in a little house with a picket fence badly in need of painting. He goes to school not so much for his edumacation but because he fancies the new girl and very much wants to impress her with his worldly knowledge, skills and charms. His best friend is a delinquent vagabond with whom the village ostracizes but he doesn't judge anybody (except maybe his half brother) and he doesn't mind skipping school now and again to explore the forests and caves with his friends. He is a born leader and even though he is not academically strong he is clever and has a way with people. No one can stay angry with him for long no matter what trouble he gets himself into.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? United 93 Didn't have the opportunity to see this on the big screen when it premiered back in ‘06. Really wish I did. However I'm certain I would've been emotionally drained afterwards. The film deals with the September 11th terrorist attacks and chronicles the last few hours of the only flight of the four hijacked planes in which the passengers managed to fight off the terrorists and prevent the plane from crashing into its intended target. The film employs the use of shaky, handheld camera which has become the signature style of its director Paul Greengrass (of whom I am of the opinion that he now overdoes this style in practically every movie he makes). The frenzied handheld style coupled with the use of real time, unknown actors, strategic camera positioning and lack of a protagonist makes the viewer feel like a random passenger aboard the flight. All of this is done intentionally by the director of course. It is one of the few movies in which, even though I knew what would be the eventual outcome, I was glued to the screen in nervous anticipation as to what was going to happen next. A very underrated movie in my honest opinion.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? When I think of a Hollywood movie that is far removed from any possible spectrum of realism, this movie always comes to my mind. You can tell by just watching the poster that this is going to be another formulaic family movie; the white background which signifies that this movie will have no content, dialogue or subplot other than this generic couple and their darned dog, the smiling figures staring at you almost sinisterly, the tepid humour of a puppy leading the couple by leash. “A dog leading its masters by leash?…….. that's so clever and ironic!” Sarcasms and cynicisms aside, here are the reasons why this movie is not just a wrong depiction of US life but an offense to ordinary people who tighten their belt and blue collar while slaving it on the 9 to 5. 1. Raising a dog = good practice for raising children, according to this movie. The above image perfectly captures how stupid that notion is. No one would watch a photo like this and and say that this is evidence of good parental skills. Besides feeding and caring there is nothing remotely similar to raising dogs as compared to children. This is a notion you tend to see solely in Hollywood movies where raising children can be condescended to the same level as keeping a litter of puppies. Raising good children, especially for poorer parents, is practically a lifelong sacrifice and the ultimate moral contract. Giving up your youth, freedom and finances and being willing to shield your child from incoming physical harm or even death is not the same as a bowl of Kibbles n Bits and a scratch on the tummy. 2. Every middle class American lives in a mansion on a sprawling well-kept spread of land. Owen Wilson and Jennifer Aniston's characters are ordinary reporters with two kids. She becomes a stay at home mom which makes him the breadwinner. His highest paying position is at The Philadelphia Inquirer which, according to online research, currently has an average annual salary of $60,000. This would mean that his monthly salary would've been around $5000 give or take. This 16 acre five bedroom Pennsylvania farmhouse had a selling price of $1.25 million in 2011. Using a mortgage calculator based on local interest rates at the time his payment for the house would’ve been roughly $5800 per month based on a 30 year loan repayment. So in other words, for the family to have realistically lived such a lifestyle, Jennifer Aniston's character had to have employed some means of soliciting tax-free money at night. 3. Let's all shed tears……. A dog has died of old age. This was the moment that was the straw that broke the camel's back. We ejected the DVD in sheer annoyance and frustration at this point. The dog died……a natural death. Cue sad music and flashbacks. How entitled can your country be if the natural death of a dog can elicit tears from an audience? A pet dog in Trinidad is lucky to live past 8 years, even in the best of care. My own backyard where I grew up contains the remains of over a dozen unfortunate cats and canines who died prematurely due to illness, speeding cars and just plain bad luck. We had not a single pet that died of natural causes i.e. old age. If we did, we would have celebrated its life and the fact that it led a full life. This supposed tearjerking scene was just another alienating Hollywoodism that highlights how out of touch the film industry is. What an awful movie full of delusional perceptions of the average American life. Don't watch it.

Why are so many men scared to date single mothers? I think the question needs to be rephrased, ‘Why are so many men scared to get seriously involved with single mothers?’ I could speak from my own personal experience of what makes me hesitant to get serious with single mothers:

Did you ever stop caring about how old you are? I remember when I was 17 and the anxiety I felt knowing that in a few months I would be a full fledged adult with responsibilities. Ripe for work life, going steady and potential marriage. Reality: I was just a kid still going to school and nothing remotely resembling a girlfriend. I remember when I was 19 how much the prospect of turning 20 meant. The big 2–0 meant that I was a ‘hardback’ man planning his career, house and family. No time for shits and giggles. Reality: This was the most immature period of my life and I was far from any kind of career, house or family. I had more time than ever for shits and giggles. I remember at 25 I observed my hairline beginning to recede. I was paranoid that I was going bald. I felt like I would be seen as a balding old perv if I chatted up 18 yo girls in the mall. I thought I was no longer a youth. Reality: I was not a balding old perv but a young man with self esteem issues. At 30 I was working two jobs trying to make ends meet. I had a daughter and was in a troubled relationship with her mother. The last thing I cared about was how old I was and I haven’t put much thought to it since almost seven years later. The moral of my story is I would’ve enjoyed my life much better if I didn’t worry about age and age expectations the way I did as a youth. I am much less bothered about turning 40 than when I was about to turn 20. When the time comes I’ll be proud to know that I was lucky to live so long.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? Recently rewatched the 2009 Star Trek film. Don't get me wrong I absolutely love this movie. I think by a long shot it is the greatest reimagining of a popular series and one of the greatest sci-fi adventures of the 21st century. However this part of the plot sticks out like a sore thumb for me. Nero, an angry and embittered Romulan from the future enacts revenge on Spock and his Vulcan race for not being able to save his planet Romulus. With his massive ship he drills a hole into the core of planet Vulcan and inserts ‘red matter’ into the core. This creates a black hole that absorbs the planet committing genocide upon the 6 billion inhabitant Vulcan race (apart from Spock, his father and a few ‘elders’). This grim aspect of the plot takes the normally light-hearted Star Trek to a whole new level of ‘shit just got serious’ seriousness. However, something about these Vulcans just don't add up. The Planet Vulcan Spock and the Vulcan race are supposed to be one of the most intelligent race of beings in the galaxy. One of their biggest traits is to maintain logic over emotion at all times. They store and process information at a volume and speed exponentially greater than humans, they are adept at learning and transmitting knowledge and their analytical skills and foresight would make living Chess legend Magnus Carlsen look like a baboon playing with his toy. Yet look at where they live. This shithole is planet Vulcan. As you can see it is a wasteland full of rocks and sand. As brilliant as these Vulcans are, their architecture looks like a bombed out Cairo at best. Vulcans are humanoid. They need food, water and sex to procreate. They admire beauty, they fall in love and they have something of a sense of humour. Their planet looks to be 20% water within a huge, dry continent devoid of vegetation of any sort. How did their population manage to reach six billion living on a hot, arid and infertile planet? Why did they never decided to colonize a more agreeable and unoccupied planet? I'm pretty sure the Federation would allow it. If they are so advanced in technology why can't they properly develop their planet and find means of increasing and distributing their water supply or getting some trees to grow? Are the Vulcan's really that smart? The Vulcans have the ability to create black holes at an instant yet they have zero defense against Romulan ships blasting holes deep into the core of their planet. They have no planetary shield, no defense satellite, no space army, they don't even have ships to escort their people off the planet. They depend entirely on Starfleet to repel the enemy and evacuate the people. Yet we're supposed to believe them to be creatures of the highest logic. The Vulcans have sent a distress call to Starfleet about their planet being attacked. I'm guessing the distress call was a bit like this: ‘Hey bros send help. Some idiot is drilling a hole into our crappy planet. It's making a lot of noise and really annoying.’ ‘Hey sorry. Forgot to warn you that they have a massive ship, 50 times bigger than the biggest Starfleet warship and using technology and weaponry that is so powerful that it most likely comes from the future. ‘Hope you sent warships and the Starfleet army and not just your student trainees and scout ships…..you did! Crap.’ ‘We’ll just go offer our prayers to our giant stone idols in our primitive church cave where you can't get a signal to beam us to safety.’ ‘If anything just send Spock to come get us.’ That aspect of the film is so utterly ludicrous that it takes me out of the movie a tad bit. Great movie nonetheless.

How do you pretend to be poor even though you are not? The poverty culture in Trinidad is different to the rest of the Western world in many aspects but in many aspects it is quite the same. If you are well-off but want to pretend that you are poor in my country (which is actually a good idea) there are several tricks of the trade you MUST adhere to. Learn the subtle art of shutting up. If you are poor you’re not supposed to have the energy to be outspoken about your interests, dreams, ideals etc. Poor people conversation is full of profound silences, minute observations and reflections of good times gone by. Idealism has no place in the conversation among a group of poor, working class Trinidadians. Stifle that urge to discuss art, complex political theory, technology, flora and fauna, science and your Utopian ideals. Deactivate. Never, at any given time, should you utter the following words/phrases while conversing with the average poor person: ethical farming, gourmet foods, non-profit organisations, recycling, 100% cotton, whole grain, organic, fair trade, energy-saving, environmentally friendly, catch and release fishing, walk-in closet, petitioning, neutering, charity of your choice, frequent flyer, volunteering, free range chickens, going green, pet insurance, shoe rack, wine rack, brunch, fuel economy. I'm not stereotyping. Poorer Trinis spend the majority of their days thinking about survival and activities associated with eradicating boredom. The above topics are usually associated with the Trinidadian upper classes. Just a mention of any such word/phrase and your poverty disguise comes into question. Let it be. Poor people quirks are shockingly different from non-poor people quirks. The more shocked and concerned you appear upon discovering quirks of your fellow less fortunate, the less genuine you seem as a poor person. Non-poor person quirk ‘Susan sure is quirky. I invited her over to lunch again. She always repeats her questions and gives a nervous laugh whenever I answer her. Plus she always rinses over my washed dishes for some reason.’ Poor person quirk ‘Jimmy sure is a character. He just killed his rooster because he said it has eyes like Hitler and now he’s out back digging a tunnel for God knows what. I wonder if he could loan me a pack of cigarettes.’ Unless a poor person’s behavior affects his family and neighbours in a negative manner, his peers simply let it be. Do not try to understand the logic in your fellow poor people’s behaviour and actions. Do not try to attempt any psychological evaluation. Do not try to lecture Billy on the dangers of gambling. Do not try to couple counsel Fred and Martha who always have a vicious fight after having sex on Sundays. Don’t try to convince Bruno that World War 3 hasn’t already begun and that it’s not taking place online. Just let it be. Embrace Fridays. There is something about Friday evenings that is almost sanctimonious with poorer working class Trini males. Regardless if there isn’t a cent in his pocket, regardless if the bank or creditors are hunting for his head, he has to ‘live’ and Friday evenings are his time to do it. If binge watching Netflix is your idea of spending your Friday evening in a working class neighborhood, everyone around you will regard you with Cold War level suspicion. Go outside and ‘lime’ (hang out), play a game of All-Fours (cards), drink or simply take a chance at the Lotto (National Lottery). Make sure and wear your best ‘liming’ clothes. You will be accepted in no time. Learn to talk the talk. Get acquainted with all the best working class quotes, parables and quips e.g. ‘It is what is,’ ‘It was his/her time,’ ‘When the cat’s away the mice begin to play.’ Every poor person uses them. Every poor person cherishes them. Learn when to use them. If you keep spewing quotes and parables every time you open your mouth you’ll be looked upon as brain damaged, or trying too hard. Here are some famous Trini working class quotes, quips and parables: ‘Yuh done know.’ (You got it) ‘He not easy.’ (He’s an asshole) ‘Monkey know which tree to climb.’ (Opportunists know who to target) ‘Wha’ yuh go do?’ (Such is life) ‘Don’t be an imps.’ (Stand up for yourself) Learn them well and observe when and how to use them. You’ll be respected and loved in no time. Here are some helpful (but optional) bits of advice to complete the disguise: Have one expensive pair of shoes that you cherish and take great care of. Wear it on Fridays. Do not leave the beach until the sun is completely gone. Never refuse charity or offerings. Even if you don’t need it. Always have that one big regret in your life. Be vocal about it among peers. NEVER buy new tires for your car. NEVER buy brand-name dog-food. Always borrow something from your neighbour and have him/her have to ask you back for it. Always be aware of what numbers played in the lottery. Never throw away clothes. Act as though you know nothing about online shopping, smart devices and ‘the Internet’ in general. Always be able to recognize if a stranger enters the neighbourhood. Memorize the vehicle model and license plate of his vehicle. Be friendly to but wary of that stranger. With all these factors in place your transformation will be complete. WE WELCOME YOU

What are some examples of excellent scenes in generally terrible movies? Joe Dirt (2001) has been savaged by critics for over two decades but in my honest opinion some of the most wittiest and well written comedic scenes can be found in this movie alongside some of its more gross and low brow. Two scenes from this movie are continuously etched in my memory. Joe Dirt (David Spade) is an atypical, Southern rock loving, beaten up car driving, mulleted redneck. He is trying to find his parents who misplaced him as a child. On his journey he travels to Indiana and encounters a creepy man who agrees he saw them at the Grand Canyon and Joe is invited inside the man's house. The scene then cuts to Joe (possibly) naked in a deep pit whilst the other man is now in drag and lingerie commanding him to put lotion on his skin whilst sitting with his little dog at the top of the pit. Joe sees nothing strange about the whole ordeal and simply asks periodically for automotive trading magazines for the past two weeks imprisonment. Joe manages to escape by police intervening at the last minute. The man is revealed to be notorious serial killer Buffalo Bob and that he was intent on flaying Joe alive to make a skin coat. None of this seems to be of any major concern for Joe except that idea was ‘gross’ and that Buffalo Bob came across ‘a little fruity.’ I honestly think this is one of the best parodies ever done so much that I've watched it on Youtube more than the actual Buffalo Bill ‘It puts the lotion on the skin’ scene from Silence of the Lambs. All props goes to actor Brian Thompson whose rendition of Buffalo Bill gives the original a run for his money. Further into the movie Joe is employed as a local school janitor in Louisiana. He befriends another janitor Clem (Christopher Walker) who is clearly an Italian American former gangster hiding from the mob under a pseudonym. Being slow witted, Joe accidentally gets Clem to be put on local television which alerts Clem's former mob associates to his whereabouts whereby they arrive the very night and shoot him up inside his house. Joe, visits the house the next day and and learns that Clem was actually Anthony Benedetti. He feels that he was indirectly responsible for Clem's death. In grief he goes to Clem's body at the scene of the crime whilst covered on a stretcher. He then begins describing how Clem would be rejoining his wife in heaven and erotically describes her body. This causes an erection to show on the corpse, revealing that Clem is actually alive. Clem reveals that he managed to kill his assailants in a shoot out and that he's faked his death to thwart the mob once again, going under the new alias of Gert. B. Frobe. It's a scene that just so outrageously silly yet believable that it sounds like one of those really good pub stories we hear that's actually based on a true story. It's also the scene that made me a fan of Christopher Walken. It's a pity that Walken hasn't been involved in more comedy films like this as I consider this his greatest role since The Deer Hunter.

What is the best case of “You just picked a fight with the wrong person” that you've witnessed? Some years ago I worked in a pretty rough school in a pretty rough neighborhood. I worked in the school library which wasn’t really a popular hangout for the dangerous kids. At least that's what I thought. There were these two boys, Jesse and Adrian who would usually remain in the library well after school hours. Jesse (16) came from a nearby projects. He was athletic and strong. He worked construction on weekends to help his family. He was around 6’2 and sinewy. Just imagine a younger Deontay Wilder without the facial hair and you had Jesse. Adrian was 16 also. He was 5’9, stocky and a video game enthusiast. He wore glasses, had a silly smile with a chipped front tooth and a prominent paunch, quite unusual for a boy his age. Just imagine Emmitt Smith with glasses and you had Adrian. Both of them couldn’t be more opposite. Jesse was thoughtful and polite. He didn’t talk much but when he did it was usually of a philosophical nature. He had a lot of ambition and was determined to make it in life. Adrian was aloof and untethered. He talked a lot and when he did it was always a lot of shit. It seemed all he knew in life were action movies, anime and video games. He had zero ambition. He cared nothing for his future, let alone his school work. Jesse came after school to the library to spend quality time with his girlfriend every once in a while. Adrian came to the library every day to play Halo and Quake III on the library computers with his gamer buddies or by himself. Jesse would come and chat with his girl in private. He never bothered anyone and if we saw any handsy-pansy going on we spoke to him about it and he would obey. Adrian would sometimes be a nuisance. Video games were not allowed but we would give the boys a chance after school hours if they behaved themselves and obeyed us. Adrian would usually overdo it and have us shut off the computers and send him home. One particular evening Jesse was alone in the library studying for the upcoming end of term exams. His girlfriend and him were going through some problems that day so he was alone and not in the best of moods. Adrian came solo as well to play video games. We told him no. He then told us he wanted to finish his assignment on the computer. We allowed him but every few minutes we took our eyes off him he would put on his video games. We could not allow this especially as exams drew near. We told him if we caught him one more time he would not only have to leave but be banned for the rest of the term. All of this childishness from Adrian was starting to get on Jesse's nerves. Some minutes after our final warning Jesse observed that Adrian was playing a juvenile video game from a web browser. He had the web page minimized at a corner of the screen to hide it from being seen. Jesse took it upon himself to deal with Adrian. Before we could say anything Jesse grabbed the mouse from Adrian’s hand and flung it aside. He then rolled Adrian and his chair away from the computer and spun it around to face him. Jesse looked as though he was going to pull Adrian off the chair by the collar. It was Jesse's biggest mistake. He severely underestimated how strong Adrian was. Adrian rose from his seat and fired two tremendous hooks, left and right, onto Jesse’s cheek and head. I could feel the power from those punches by just looking at them and I knew that the fight was over before it even began. Jesse struggled to keep to his feet and attempted to wrestle Adrian to the ground. It was no good. The punches had him dazed. Adrian easily shook him off and was about to land some more until he saw myself and my coworker coming to subdue him. Adrian had momentarily transformed from a goofy nerd into Mike Tyson for a few seconds. He left the scene immediately. We had to subdue Jesse who claimed that he was going after Adrian to teach him a lesson for the ‘sucker punch.’ We all knew that was just talk. Jesse didn't want to face that beast again. No one in their right mind would. Jesse didn't report the matter and requested the same of us, clearly due to embarrassment. With his naturally forgiving nature Jesse had no hard feelings and the boys developed a mutual respect after. Jesse graduated from the school with some decent grades and works as a successful salesman and party promoter. Adrian graduated from the school with nothing but a superb left and right hook. I truly hope he used his power to good use.

Who is an actor who you think looks better older than they did when they were younger? To me, she looked like the girl in class who you'd keep in mind as 2nd choice if your crush rejected you.
